When Did Medical Innovation Become a Bad Thing?

Coke Morgan Stewart

8 hours ago   0

Share

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:30
Instaread

“Genuine abuses deserve scrutiny. But counting patents, criticizing improvements, and treating new formulations as inherently suspicious risks confusing innovation with misconduct.”

Congress has been holding hearings on pharmaceutical patents and drug prices, along with U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) fee-setting and oversight. During these hearings, America’s pharmaceutical innovators face an unusual criticism: They are accused of abusing the patent system not only when they invent new medicines, but also when they improve them.

Critics have developed an entire vocabulary for this supposed problem. Multiple patents become “patent thickets.” Improvements to existing medicines become “evergreening.” Introducing new formulations becomes “product hopping.”

As a former Acting Director and Deputy Director of the USPTO, and now President and CEO of the Council for Innovation Promotion (C4IP), I have seen firsthand how important it is to distinguish legitimate innovation from actual abuses of the patent system.

These labels are, as President Trump likes to say, “fake news.” They have been made up to hide a more nuanced discussion of the legal and technical requirements for patenting.

Let’s examine each narrative.

False Narrative #1: Patent Thickets are Evidence of Abuse.

The argument is simple: When a pharmaceutical company holds numerous patents associated with a single medicine, it must be creating a thicket designed to block competitors.

I see a different image. Not a thicket but a garden of complementary patents that grow where innovation leads.

Those seeking to copy medicines as generics undoubtedly want to find a shortcut through that garden—often by mowing it down. But the garden reflects the complexities of the innovation process itself. There are no shortcuts to developing a new drug that is effective and safe—a process that often costs in the billions, with many candidates failing along the way.

On top of that, these patent gardens encourage “designing around”—an important aspect of the patent system that creates additional innovations.

False Narrative #2: Evergreening Allows Companies to Extend Patents Indefinitely.

The accusation is that pharmaceutical companies make minor changes to existing medicines to continually extend their original patent.

This, too, is wrong. A patent on an improvement does not extend the term of the earlier patent. New patents are for new inventions. Generics are free to copy the earlier version when the original patents covering them expire.

But quite often, the improvements—protected by new patents—offer substantial benefits that doctors and patients prefer. This is not an “extension” of the original patent; it is an entirely new invention or set of inventions.

Additionally, related patents or “patent families” do not have endless terms. Often these patents are related because they are derived from the same initial patent application. That means each of these patents are tied to the same priority date—the date that counts for purposes of calculating when the patent expires. If anything, that requirement shortens the life of related patents because they have the same expiration date even if they are filed later in time.

And there are even more restrictions. If a single claim in a related patent is substantially similar to a claim in another patent, all the claims receive a shortened term through a terminal disclaimer. On top of that, the terminal disclaimer restricts who can assert the related patent to one party, so that related inventions aren’t asserted separately.

False Narrative #3: Product Hopping is a Strategy to Prevent Generic Competition.

Similar to accusations of evergreening, when a pharmaceutical company introduces a new version of an existing medicine, critics may accuse it of product hopping.

But that new version might reduce dosing frequency, improve patient adherence, or offer meaningful therapeutic benefits. For example, an injection you need in the hospital might become a pill you can take at home. It is easy to overlook the difficulty of developing such innovations and the value—and cost savings—that they bring to patients. Meanwhile, the earlier version becomes available for generics to manufacture.

Patients want medical advances, and they want choices. If we demonize new versions of existing medicines, we won’t just harm innovation, we will harm medical outcomes for the people who depend on them.

Fake Slogans Threaten Innovation

None of this means every pharmaceutical patent is valid or every business practice is lawful. Genuine abuses deserve scrutiny. But counting patents, criticizing improvements, and treating new formulations as inherently suspicious risks confusing innovation with misconduct.

Today’s new drugs, protected for a limited time, ensure the low-cost generics of our future. It’s time to stop attacking medical innovation with fake slogans.
